difficultyRationale: A foundational distinction, but one teams still get wrong when scaling under write-heavy load.
prompt: A team is seeing their primary database struggle under load and adds several read replicas, routing all SELECT queries to them. A month later, the service is still slow — but now it's specifically because writes are backing up, not reads. What does this reveal about what read replicas actually scale?
explanation: Read replicas scale read capacity by letting multiple replicas each independently serve SELECT queries. They do nothing for write capacity: every write still has to go through the single primary (replicas only receive already-committed changes from it), so a write-heavy bottleneck is completely unaffected by adding more replicas.

options.text: Read replicas only add capacity for read queries; every write still has to be processed by the one primary database and then propagated outward, so a write-throughput bottleneck is untouched no matter how many replicas are added.
options.explanation: Correct. Replicas are read-only copies kept in sync from the primary — adding more of them increases how many SELECT queries the system can serve concurrently, but does nothing to increase how many writes the primary itself can accept.

options.text: Read replicas do scale write throughput too, but only after a configurable delay during which writes are buffered locally — the team's problem is simply that this buffering window hasn't been tuned long enough yet for their workload.
options.explanation: Read replicas don't accept or buffer writes at all in a standard replica setup; they are read-only by design, so there is no write-buffering delay to tune — the write bottleneck is at the primary itself, not a configuration gap on the replicas.

options.text: The write slowdown is actually caused by the replicas themselves competing with the primary for the same underlying disk I/O bandwidth, so removing replicas (not adding more) would be the correct fix for this write bottleneck.
options.explanation: Replicas typically run on separate instances/storage from the primary specifically to avoid this kind of resource contention; the write slowdown is explained simply by write volume exceeding what the single primary can process, independent of replica count.

options.text: This is expected: adding read replicas always temporarily increases write latency for the first few weeks while the replication topology stabilizes, and the slowdown will resolve itself once that stabilization period fully completes.
options.explanation: There's no such self-resolving 'stabilization period' effect on write latency from adding read replicas; a sustained write bottleneck reflects the primary's actual write capacity limit, not a temporary topology-settling artifact.
